chapter_theme: Paalai: the dry spring of murukku, kongam and pungu that marks the season of return (63-67, 79-80); the man who cannot leave for her glance (68); the friend's and the heroine's arguments for and against going for wealth, from manly duty to youth that will not come back (82-87, 91-92); and the eloped girl seen on the road by villagers and travellers, and mourned and sought by her mother among trees and diviners (65, 69-73, 75, 81, 88-90).

63.reading: The friend asks the heroine, whose paired breasts are like kongam buds dressed in gold, why, now that striped bees sing over every fire-red cluster of the asoka, her shoulders with their flower bangles wear this matchless pallor.
63.nuance: The question answers itself: the asoka in flower is the season he named, so her pallor marks that he has not come. என்னணிந்த makes the pallor something she has put on, set against the gold the kongam wears.

thinai_evidence.note: the asoka and kongam in flower, the trees of the dry spring

comparisons.tenor: her paired breasts with their golden spots, seen as gold-decked kongam buds

64.reading: Though she is told to keep herself in hand she will not, so the friend bids the girl of modest, fine bangles look at the shamelessness of the season: the moist murukku blazing as if fire had been scattered, the pungu white as if puffed rice had been strewn.
64.nuance: நாணிண்மை is read as நாண் இன்மை; whether the shamelessness is the trees' open display or the girl's open grieving turns on that reading. Either way it is set against her own modesty in நாணாய நல்வளையாய்.

thinai_evidence.note: murukku and pungu in bloom, the flowers of the paalai spring

comparisons.tenor: the murukku's red blossom, as if fire were scattered
the pungu's white blossom, as if puffed rice were strewn

65.reading: The mother searching for her eloped daughter speaks to the dark kuravam: you bore your doll-flowers while the kongam, sagging, gave them the breast as foster mother; though you will not speak to me as one mother to another, come and show me the way my sharp-toothed girl went.
65.nuance: The kuravam's flower was called பாவை, doll, so the speaker sees a tree that bore a child and had another nurse it, which is the household's own arrangement of mother and foster mother; she asks the tree for ஈன்றாள் மொழி, the word a mother owes a mother. The addressee is the tree.

thinai_evidence.note: a mother asking the way her daughter took with her lover

comparisons.tenor: a foster mother nursing a child, the kongam bud as the breast
the kuravam's flower as a daughter it has borne

66.reading: The friend tells the heroine he will come soon: look, all the murukku trees, shining, have chosen and set gold talis over fine coral shoots, like goldsmiths making ornaments for rich men's children.
66.nuance: The goldsmith simile makes the season a craftsman delivering on time (தேர்ந்து, choosing carefully), so the trees' punctuality stands surety for the man's.

thinai_evidence.note: the murukku in bloom, the season of his promised return

comparisons.tenor: the murukku trees, working their blossoms like goldsmiths making ornaments to order
the red shoots and golden buds of the murukku

67.reading: The heroine tells her friend that the man who went for wealth has not appeared; if she is told to bear it, can it be borne? The paired murukku blossoms, like coral set in gold, seem to punish her, and the sickness within her is great.
67.nuance: வெறுக்கை, wealth, is the word the verse opens on, and நோய் the word it ends on: the trade of one for the other is the whole complaint.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone for wealth and she waits

comparisons.tenor: the murukku blossom, red set in gold
the flowering murukku as one who punishes her

68.reading: The man asks his heart what way there is to go when, as he stands in the great wasteland, the meaning in the glance of the young girl who loves her jewels, her eyes reaching to her earrings, stays and will not let him go.
68.nuance: A செலவழுங்குதல் poem: the journey is undone not by her words but by the குறிப்பு of a glance, which he reads only once he is already on the road. ஒளிவிடா (does not let go, or does not cease to shine) is read loosely.

thinai_evidence.note: the man weighing a journey across the waste

69.reading: Villagers tell the eloping man that the road is long and the fiery sun has already sunk half his red disc behind the western hill, so it would be fitting for him to stay the night in their small village with this jewelled girl and go on tomorrow in proper order.
69.nuance: அத்தம் is used twice in one line with two senses, the road and the hill of sunset, so a single word names both the danger and the hour; the offer is shelter for a couple who have left their kin.

thinai_evidence.note: the long road at sunset

70.reading: On the road the man tells the girl to see the deer with her look resting in the cool kuravam shade and the flowering kongam with the look of gold, and calls her, a slender branch with soft breasts decked in golden spots, to come and play at sand houses on the sand.
70.nuance: வண்டல் அயர் is the girls' game of sand houses she has left at home; he offers her the wasteland as that playground, so the comfort is for the life she gave up.

thinai_evidence.note: kuravam and kongam of the dry spring

comparisons.tenor: the deer whose eyes have the girl's look
the kongam flower with the colour of gold
the girl, slender as a branch

71.reading: Seeing the jewelled girl, her face bright as the midnight moon, and the man of the long spear, hot-bright as the sun, walking along together, onlookers cried out in fear that both lights had come down and the world, left with neither, would lie desolate.
71.nuance: The hyperbole puts sun and moon on one road, which the sky never allows; the onlookers' fear is praise. மாநிலா in line 2 is hard to place and is read with the man's sun-image only loosely.

thinai_evidence.note: onlookers watching an eloping couple pass

comparisons.tenor: the couple as moon and sun

72.reading: Taking her face for a lotus, her smile for an ambal, her eyes for blue lilies and her fingers for kaanthal, the bees gather over her in delight and make a shade, so the simple girl goes on her way pleasantly, without suffering.
72.nuance: The bees' mistake turns her beauty into shelter: the four flowers belong to the watered fields and the hills, not the waste, so she carries a cooler land with her and is shaded by it. The speaker is not named; onlookers reassuring the foster mother fits the closing line.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl going on the road with her lover

comparisons.tenor: her face as a lotus
her smile as the white ambal
her eyes as blue lilies
her fingers as kaanthal

73.reading: The mother laments that her simple girl, with red mouth and dark eyes, has gone off and given up the garlanded parrot of her playmates, whose speech was like hers, and the blue lily of the cool pond, which was like her eyes, unable to bear the town's gossip.
73.nuance: The parrot and the lily are the things her mouth and eyes were praised by; the mother counts it a loss that the girl no longer needs her likenesses. The run of negatives in lines 1 and 2 (கேளாதும், காணாதும், ஆற்றாதும்) is read only loosely.

thinai_evidence.note: the mother of a girl who has left home

comparisons.tenor: the girl's speech, matched with the parrot's
the girl's dark eyes, matched with the blue lily

74.reading: The heroine tells a small dove not to sulk with its mate, since sulking is no matter even between those bound in love: he hardened and left, and she bids it look at the road he went by and at her own colour, now turned to gold from watching it.
74.nuance: The warning may carry a confession: her own sulking came before his going. The dove pair is addressed and the moral is spoken aloud, so it is neither ullurai (the tenor is stated) nor iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: watching the road he left by

comparisons.tenor: the pallor that has covered her like gold

75.reading: The mother says the road her girl took behind the man of slaying strength is the long wasteland where the sun burns with matchless rays, not sparing her loosened hair, and where the python lies dying, limp as a twisted rope let go.
75.nuance: The heat kills even the python that lies in wait for travellers, so the mother's fear passes from the beast to the sun. Line 2 (விரிந்து விடுகூந்தல் வெஃகா) is a repaired line whose reading differs from the web witness, and its sense is guessed.

thinai_evidence.note: the long waste under the burning sun

comparisons.tenor: the python lying limp, like a rope let go

76.reading: The friend tells the man that, on the long waste where paddy would pop into puffed rice at the mere thought of it, she was afraid of the road even when told not to fear, and tears filled her long spear-like eyes, slit wide to her ears.
76.nuance: The hyperbole (grain pops at a thought) puts the heat in the mind before the body; whose fear அஞ்சிற்று names, and whether the speaker is the friend, is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the waste so hot that grain would pop

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, long and sharp as weapons

77.reading: The heroine asks her slender-waisted friend whether, when he comes, she cannot go with him across the long bamboo waste that looks burnt by the sun's long rays, and recalls the look given as she set out, her fragrant hair tumbling, her trailing robe gathered in her hand, her makara earring turned back.
77.nuance: Who gave the look of lines 3 and 4 (தந்தார்) and to whom is not clear; the reading takes it as the picture of a girl setting out with her lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-scorched bamboo waste

comparisons.tenor: the bamboo waste, looking as if burnt

78.reading: The heroine prays that the man who went into the hill waste, where even the great elephant with one trunk, two tusks and three musth streams finds no water to drink in the green spring, turns off the path and falls, may come to no harm.
78.nuance: The counting conceit (one, two, three) builds the elephant up only to fell it, so the wish அழிவிலர் ஆக asks for more than the land allows. Not iraicchi: the elephant is alone and does nothing a lover does.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill waste whose springs are dry

79.reading: The friend tells the tight-bangled heroine, who will not trust those who stand by her, that the return of the man who went is not far off: let her see, without delay, the hill country where the shining waterfall shows like the banner raised by victors.
79.nuance: The victors' banner makes the waterfall announce his success before he arrives; the falls run full only when the rains he promised to return by have come.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting for the man's return from his journey

comparisons.tenor: the waterfall, white and streaming as a victors' banner

80.reading: The friend tells the heroine of spear-fine eyes that the man who went far to bring wealth will come today in honour across the long waste where things have shrivelled and dropped in dread of the lord of the one-wheeled chariot, for this is the hour her left eye throbs.
80.nuance: இடம் closes the verse in two senses, place and the left side: the throbbing of a woman's left eye is the good omen, so the poem ends on the sign, not the road.

thinai_evidence.note: the long waste under the sun

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, sharp and bright as a spear
the sun, lord of the one-wheeled chariot

81.reading: The mother of the girl who has gone speaks to the konrai, the kuruntham and the mullai creeper: you have withered; I stand here and I know; what did you say to the long-eyed girl as she went, and what did she say to you, leaving with her lightning-bright ornaments glittering?
81.nuance: The stammered question of line 3 (என்னுரைத்தீர்க்கு என்னுரைத்தாட்கு...) puts the grief into the syntax. The withered mullai plants may be read as having withered at the girl's going.

thinai_evidence.note: the mother of a girl who has eloped

comparisons.tenor: her ornaments, flashing like lightning

82.reading: The friend tells the soft-spoken heroine that men, weighing the way that is a man's duty, have taken it up and cherished it as a duty they must bear, and so will go to make wealth; it is good that she not go even a little into wasting grief.
82.nuance: கடன் is said three times (ஆண்கடன், பூண்கடன் twice): the comfort is an argument from obligation, which casts the heroine's grief as a lapse from her own duty to bear it.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going for wealth

83.reading: The heroine asks whether he would really go: even the thought is unbearable and her heart burns; will he who went win and finish his work? She bids her friend hear the cicadas that wander and shrill like a doe crying at a beast of stone.
83.nuance: The simile of lines 3 and 4 is obscure (இதடி, கல் மா); the reading follows the plain words, a doe calling at something that will never answer, which fits a voice crying to an absent man.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going on his work

comparisons.tenor: the cicadas' shrilling, like a doe crying at a beast of stone

84.reading: The heroine asks whether men with someone of their own would thrust her aside and go by the track of graceless warriors, who rush out and shoot travellers even when they carry no wealth to take, in the cactus scrub where the wild bison flees.
84.nuance: அருளில் sets the robbers' lack of grace beside the man's own: he goes for wealth by a road where others kill those who have none, and the parallel is left for the hearer.

thinai_evidence.note: the cactus scrub of the waste

85.reading: The man who keeps saying 'wealth, wealth' has treasured those words like gold until grace counts for nothing; since he has a way to bring wealth back, let him agree to bring back youth as well.
85.nuance: The taunt rests on what it leaves unsaid: wealth can be fetched again, youth cannot, so his own reasoning about wealth refutes his going.

thinai_evidence.note: the man resolved on going for wealth

comparisons.tenor: his talk of wealth, held as precious as gold

86.reading: The heroine tells her friend, who said he would surely go, to name anyone who could bear it, and calls her excellent indeed, when he would hurry across the waste where a worn-out elephant that can go no farther eyes men in its hunger and eats.
86.nuance: சிறந்தாயே is irony. ஆள் பார்த்து மிசைந்தொழியும் is read literally, though an elephant eating men is odd; the sense may be that it waits by the path for travellers.

thinai_evidence.note: the waste of the starving elephant

87.reading: The friend asks whether they can say even one word against the going of the man who guards his fame and never turns back: the far waste is hard to cross even as companion to that unconquerable young spearman, skilled with the bow.
87.nuance: The repeated பின்றா (not turning back) is made his virtue and the reason no one can hold him; whether the heroine is being told she could not go with him is not clear.

thinai_evidence.note: the far waste he will cross

88.reading: Speaking of her elder brothers' disapproval, which the heroine of long sword-like eyes will not accept, the friend seems to warn her that if she holds back now he will embrace her once and go away offended.
88.nuance: The first two lines are hard to construe; the reading rests on ஐயன்மார் (elder brothers), வல்லி ஒழியின் (if you fail to be firm) and புல்லி ஒழிவான் புலந்து (he will embrace and leave, sulking).

thinai_evidence.note: the brothers' opposition and the lover's possible leaving

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, long and sharp as a sword

89.reading: Travellers answer the searching mother: go on close behind them, for if they are your people your purpose will not come easily; I saw the man like the hot sun, and she saw the girl like the cool moon.
89.nuance: The sighting is divided by sex: the man saw the man and his woman companion saw the girl, a propriety of the road; sun and moon make the couple a matched pair. Line 2's எண்ணிய எண்ணம் எளிதரா is read only tentatively.

thinai_evidence.note: travellers who have seen the eloping pair

comparisons.tenor: the man, bright and hot as the sun
the girl, bright and cool as the moon

90.reading: The mother asks the diviner apart, by his god, to tell her, since telling is his gift: will the youth bring the girl of victorious bangles first up to her house, or take her straight to his own?
90.nuance: வேறாக, said twice, frames the question as private: the mother asks apart because the answer (his house, not hers) would shame her before others. The addressee is the diviner.

thinai_evidence.note: the mother of an eloped girl asking where the wedding will be

91.reading: The heroine asks whether men who mean to live would go near a place of cactus, dark omai, long murungai with fibreless flowers and bamboo, where the spotted kite and the vulture watch for travellers and sit there sleeping till they die.
91.nuance: The birds' patience is the horror: they sit and doze because the travellers will die without their help. நற்றிய and நாரில்பூ are uncertain words, and வாழ்பவர் may mean those who wish to live or those who live well.

thinai_evidence.note: cactus, omai and carrion birds of the waste

92.reading: The heroine asks whether a man would go, ruining the well-being of those who depend on him, by the road where cicadas crowd and shrill as if to kill under the hot sun, the dust swells and burns, the sky scorches from above and from below the feet burn and the eyes smart.
92.nuance: தம்மடைந்தார் (those who have come to him for refuge) makes the wife a dependant, so his going is a breach of the protector's duty, not only of love; the heat is mapped above, below and in the eyes.

thinai_evidence.note: the road under the burning sun

comparisons.tenor: the cicadas' shrilling, as if they were killing

links.note: Kalittokai 33: in spring the silk-cotton flowers like fire and the pungu sheds blossom like puffed rice (எரி உரு உறழ இலவம், பொரி உரு உறழப் புன்கு), and the heroine feels the season mock the lonely. Thinaimalai 64 gives the murukku as scattered fire and the pungu as scattered puffed rice.
links.teaches: The pungu as puffed rice is fixed across both poems while the fire moves from silk-cotton to murukku, and the same paired images serve the heroine's complaint in Kalittokai and the friend's rebuke of open grieving in the venba, so the spring catalogue was a shared stock that either speaker could turn.

links.note: Akananuru 369: the foster mother grieves that since the girl left, the parrot will not drink its milk, her playmates do not play and the doll gets no offering. Thinaimalai 73: the mother says the girl has given up her playmates' parrot and the pond's blue lily.
links.teaches: Read together they give both sides of the break: in the Akananuru the home's things go without the girl, in the venba the girl has already let go of the things her beauty was measured by, so the mother's grief covers both what the house lost and what the daughter chose.

links.note: Kalittokai 11: the heroine reasons that the man will return because he told her the burning forest holds a tusker that lets its mate drink the little muddy water first, a dove that fans its mate and a stag that shades its doe. Thinaimalai 78: an elephant alone finds no water in the spring and falls.
links.teaches: The same waterless road gives comfort in Kalittokai 11 and fear in the venba, and the difference is whether the poet gives the elephant a mate: the paired beast turns drought into proof of tenderness, the lone beast only into a measure of danger.

links.note: Kalittokai 11 closes its argument that the man will return with the omens at home: the lizard chirps on the good side and her lovely eye throbs on the left (உண் கண்ணும் ஆடுமால், இடனே). Thinaimalai 80 ends on the same left-eye omen, with the same closing word இடம்.
links.teaches: Kalittokai 11 reaches the throbbing left eye only after a long proof from the man's own words, while the venba rests the promise of return on the omen alone, which shows the left-eye sign was a recognised closing proof that could carry a whole short poem.

links.note: Kuruntokai 135: the friend tells the heroine not to cry: the man himself said work is life to men and men are life to women of the house, so he will put off his going. Thinaimalai 82: the friend says a man's duty makes him go for wealth, so she should not grieve. On the plain reading the two friends draw opposite conclusions from the same premise.
links.teaches: Both friends begin from the maxim that work belongs to men, but the Kuruntokai adds that men are women's life and concludes he will stay, while the venba stops at the man's duty and concludes he will go, so the outcome turns entirely on whether the maxim's second half is said.

links.note: Purananuru 312 assigns each person a கடன்: bearing the son is the mother's, making him worthy the father's, and killing elephants in battle the young man's. Thinaimalai 82 calls going to make wealth the man's கடன், repeating the word three times.
links.teaches: The venba carries the heroic vocabulary of duty from the battlefield to the trade road: what Purananuru 312 makes the young man's duty in war, the later akam friend makes his duty in wealth-making, and uses it to silence the wife's grief.

links.note: Akananuru 375: the heroine says she would not weep if she knew he passed unharmed the waste where raw youths kill even travellers without ornaments to test their arrows. Thinaimalai 84: the same robbers who shoot travellers with no wealth are the heroine's reason he should not go at all.
links.teaches: The robbers who kill the penniless serve the Akananuru heroine as a fear for a man already on the road and the venba's heroine as an argument against his setting out, so one road-danger supports both the anxiety after departure and the plea before it.

links.note: Kalittokai 15 ends a long plea with the argument that wealth can be made any day, but asks whether it can bring back youth once it has passed (வளமையோ வைகலும் செயல் ஆகும் ... இளமையும் தருவதோ). Thinaimalai 85 builds its whole verse on the same contrast of வளமை and இளமை.
links.teaches: The venba condenses into four lines the closing move of a long Kalittokai paalai, keeping even the rhyme of வளமை and இளமை, which shows that the retort had become a fixed argument of the separation poem that needed no road scene to carry it.

links.note: Naladiyar 11: knowing grey hair will come, the wise renounce in childhood, while those who delight in fleeting youth rise later on a staff. Thinaimalai 85: because youth cannot be brought back, the man should stay with his wife rather than chase wealth. On a plain reading the same fact counsels withdrawal in one and staying for love in the other.
links.teaches: From the one premise that youth does not return, the Naladiyar argues for leaving pleasure early and the paalai friend for keeping it while it lasts, so the impermanence of youth was an argument that served the householder's love as readily as the renouncer's flight.

links.note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Thinaimalai 86: told that he will surely go, the heroine says to name anyone who could bear it.
links.teaches: Both meet the news of his going by sending the message elsewhere, to whoever can survive it, and the venba supplies the starving elephant's waste that the couplet leaves out, so the Kural's bare retort is shown to be the stock reply of the paalai heroine to the announcement of departure.

links.note: Kalittokai 9: the mother asks travelling brahmins whether they saw her daughter and the youth; they say they did, and argue that as sandal, pearl and music serve others than their source, so the daughter belongs to the man she followed. Thinaimalai 89: travellers say they saw the man like the sun and the girl like the moon.
links.teaches: The venba keeps Kalittokai 9's frame of the mother questioning travellers and their 'we saw them' but drops the brahmins' argument that a daughter belongs to her husband, so the consolation shrinks to an image of a well-matched pair, and the mother is left with a report rather than a reason.

links.note: Kuruntokai 315: the heroine says the hill man is like the sun (ஞாயிறு அனையன்) and her shoulders like the nerunji flower. Thinaimalai 89: the man is like the hot sun and the girl like the cool moon.
links.teaches: In the Kuruntokai the man as sun makes the woman a nerunji that turns after him, while in the venba she is the moon, a second light of her own, so the same sun-image yields dependence in one poem and parity in the other.

links.note: Akananuru 195: the mother of the eloped girl, after picturing the other mother preparing her house for the couple, asks the diviner whether the youth will bring the girl first to her house or take her to his own (எம்மனை முந்துறத் தருமோ? தன்மனை உய்க்குமோ?). Thinaimalai 90 asks the same question in nearly the same words.
links.teaches: The venba keeps the Akananuru mother's question almost word for word while dropping the rival mother's preparations and her own years of nursing, which shows that by the later anthology the question to the diviner had become a fixed turn of the eloped girl's mother that could stand without its reasons.

source_issues.issue: Line 2 is a repaired line (the old encoding '·' for ஃ in வெஃகா) and its reading differs from sangamtamil.com; the sense of விரிந்து விடுகூந்தல் வெஃகா is uncertain.
Line 1 splits தாமரை across a space (முகந்தா மரைமுறுவல்), apparently for the metre; read as முகம் தாமரை.
Lines 1 and 2 (அல்லாத என்னையும் தீரமற்று ஐயன்மார் பொல்லாதது) do not construe cleanly; the text may be corrupt.
நற்றியவேய் (line 2) and நாரில்பூ (line 1) are obscure; the text may be corrupt.
